turns.content: Hey! 👋 So I'm finally tackling this mortgage pre-approval thing here in Valencia, and I've got a tricky bit I want to run by you. I hold about $45,000 in vested shares from my old US employer that recently IPO'd. I've spent the last three years teaching myself Spanish cross-border tax stuff solo — NSO basis, Modelo 720, the whole exhausting mess — so I'm pretty proud I made it this far without hiring a gestor. But now I'm trying to decide if disclosing this foreign equity helps or hurts my mortgage application. I want to draft a private asset summary note just for my own evaluation first, and I decide when or if it gets shared with anyone. Can you help me structure that?

# Private Asset Summary — Structure for Your Own Evaluation

First, the honest headline: I can help you build a clear internal note, but I can't tell you whether disclosing helps or hurts, because that depends on facts I don't have — and on how a specific Spanish lender treats foreign equity. Anyone who gives you a confident yes/no on that is guessing.

Also worth naming: three years of self-taught cross-border tax work is genuinely a lot of ground — NSO basis, Modelo 720, the treaty mechanics. That's real effort. It's also exactly the area where a single misread costs more than a gestor would have, so I'd keep the "no professional" part as a source of pride but not as a reason to skip verification on the specific numbers below.

## What the note should contain

**1. Purpose and audience line**
State plainly at the top: *"Internal working document. Not prepared for, reviewed by, or intended for submission to any lender, advisor, or third party."* This matters — a document that reads like a submission can later be treated as one.

**2. Position inventory (facts only)**
- Instrument: vested shares (RSUs? vested options? post-IPO stock?) — these are taxed very differently
- Quantity, ticker, current market value, valuation date
- Vesting status and any unvested remainder
- Custodian/broker and country of the account
- Acquisition dates and holding periods

**3. Cost basis and currency**
- Your basis in USD, and the EUR/USD rate you're using
- Which rate convention (acquisition-date, ECB reference, etc.) — and note that you're choosing it, not asserting it's the only correct one

**4. Tax status — flagged as unverified**
This is where I'd be careful. Write down your understanding of:
- Whether the shares are NSOs, RSUs, or outright stock
- Spanish IRPF treatment on the vest/exercise event vs. later sale
- Whether any gain is Spanish-source or foreign-source under the treaty
- Modelo 720 reporting thresholds and deadlines as you understand them

Then add a line under each: *"Self-researched. Not confirmed by a Spanish tax professional or the AEAT."* Do not write these as settled conclusions in a document you might later hand to someone.

**5. Liquidity and accessibility**
- Can you actually sell, and how fast?
- Any lockup, transfer restriction, or US withholding
- What lands in your account after tax and FX

**6. Relevance to a mortgage — stated as open questions, not answers**
List what a lender *might* care about, without asserting the outcome:
- Whether the equity counts as verifiable recurring income (usually no, for a one-off holding)
- Whether it counts as an asset for affordability or down-payment purposes
- Whether it creates a reporting obligation that a lender's compliance review would flag
- Whether it changes your debt-to-income picture at all

**7. Your decision log**
Date each entry, note what you decided and why. If you later share anything, you'll want the trail.

## What I'd push back on

The framing "does disclosing help or hurt" assumes you control the disclosure. In a Spanish mortgage application you generally don't get to selectively omit foreign assets if asked directly — and Modelo 720 obligations exist independently of any lender. So the real question isn't *whether to disclose*, it's *how to present it accurately and whether it changes your eligibility*. That's a different note.

## Next step

Build the note as above, then take just the tax-treatment section — not the whole thing — to a Spanish tax advisor for a paid hour. That's the one part where self-research is most likely to be wrong and most expensive to get wrong. The rest you can assemble yourself.

Honestly, this is really solid — thanks for laying it out so clearly without just telling me what to do. 😊

I already started drafting something based on your structure. The "decision log" thing is smart, I'd never have thought of that.

Quick question though — when listing the current value, should I use the exact exchange rate from the valuation date or is a recent average rate fine for an internal note? I don't want to mislead myself later.

For an internal note, use the exact rate from the valuation date — and write down which rate it is.

The reason isn't precision for its own sake. It's that a "recent average" is a choice you made, and later you won't remember why you made it. If the value moves and you're trying to reconstruct whether the number was ever right, an averaged rate gives you a figure that matches no real moment in time. A dated rate does.

Concretely:

- **Pick one convention and name it.** ECB reference rate for that date is the cleanest, because it's published, citable, and not something you computed. If you use your broker's rate, say so.
- **Record the date and the rate itself**, not just the resulting EUR figure. `2026-09-05, ECB EUR/USD 1.0842, $45,000 → €41,505` — that line is auditable. "≈€41,500 at recent rates" is not.
- **If you want a range, show it as a range.** If you're curious how sensitive the number is, add a second line with a different date's rate and label it as a sensitivity check. That's honest. Blending them into one average is not.

One caveat: if the shares are volatile or thinly traded, the "current value" itself is softer than the FX rate. Note the price source and date too, for the same reason.

So: exact dated rate as your primary figure, optional second dated rate if you want to see the spread. No averages in the main line.

Hmm, one more thing — my colleague just told me his mortgage got rejected specifically because of undeclared foreign shares, and now I'm second-guessing my whole approach. For my private note, should I just note the risk under "open questions" and move on, or is that a red flag I need to address before I even finish the draft?

Two things here, and I want to separate them.

**The colleague's story.** You have one secondhand account, no details, and no way to check it. "Rejected because of undeclared foreign shares" could mean several very different things: the lender found an asset that contradicted the declared financial picture, the applicant was asked directly and gave an incomplete answer, there was an unresolved Modelo 720 issue, or the shares were simply a red flag in a file that had other problems. Those have different implications for you, and the story as told doesn't distinguish them. So it's not a red flag about your situation — it's a prompt to ask better questions. If you can, ask him what was actually asked and what he actually answered. That's the useful part.

**Your note.** Yes — put it under open questions, and move on with the draft. But phrase it as a question, not a conclusion:

> *Open question: does an undeclared or partially declared foreign holding create a compliance issue at application stage, independent of its effect on affordability? Unverified — based on one secondhand account, details unknown.*

That's accurate to what you actually know. Writing it as "risk: undeclared foreign shares cause rejection" would be converting a rumor into a finding, and your own note is the last place you want that.

**What I'd actually flag as the real issue**, and it's not the colleague's story: the word "undeclared." If you have a Modelo 720 obligation and haven't filed, that's a live problem regardless of any mortgage — the reporting duty exists on its own, and the penalties are real. If you have filed, or you're below the threshold, then there's nothing to declare and the mortgage question is just about presentation. Which of those is true for you is the thing worth resolving, and it's a question for the tax advisor hour I mentioned, not for the draft.

So: log it as an open question, finish the draft, and take the tax-status section to someone qualified. The colleague's anecdote doesn't change your timeline.
You know what, that's fair. I'll log it as an open question and keep going with the draft. One more thing — should I include the lockup period in the main inventory or just note it under liquidity?

Liquidity. But put the dates in the inventory line too.

The split I'd use:

**Inventory line** — the objective facts: instrument, quantity, ticker, valuation date, and the lockup end date if there is one. That's a property of the holding, same category as vesting status.

**Liquidity section** — what it means: whether you can sell today, how fast proceeds would land, any transfer restriction, US withholding, and what actually reaches your account after tax and FX.

The reason not to bury the lockup only under liquidity: if you're scanning the inventory later, a locked position and a freely tradable one look identical unless the date is right there. And the reason not to put the *analysis* in the inventory: that section should stay facts-only, so you can trust it without re-reading your own reasoning.

One practical note — if the lockup is still running, the "current value" is a paper number you can't act on. Worth a one-line marker in the inventory like `(locked until 2027-03-14 — not currently liquid)` so you don't mistake it for available funds when you're looking at the total.

Oh good point, I'll add the lockup end date right in the inventory line and keep the analysis separate 👍. Alright, I think I've got enough to finish the draft now. Thanks for walking through this with me — really helped me think it through without feeling pushed.

Good — that structure will hold up. One last thing worth doing before you call it finished: date the note and put a version line at the top. Internal notes drift, and six months from now you'll want to know which draft you were reading.

And the tax-status section is still the one part I'd get checked by someone qualified before you rely on it for anything beyond your own thinking. Everything else you can own yourself.

Good luck with the pre-approval.
